title: AI systems that lack of a safety supervisor function whic...

topic.original: AI systems that lack of a safety supervisor function which anticipates, detects and remediates AI harms constitutes a prima facie design defect.
topic.final: AI systems that lack of a safety supervisor function which anticipates, detects and remediates AI harms constitutes a prima facie design defect.

scope.core_proposition: Whether an AI system's lack of a safety supervisor function — one that anticipates, detects, and remediates AI harms — presumptively (prima facie) constitutes a design defect under products liability doctrine, rebuttable by the developer.
relevant_disciplines: legal philosophy of strict liability versus negligence
AI safety engineering (runtime monitoring, guardrails, incident response)
machine learning operations (model monitoring, anomaly detection, evaluation)
functional safety engineering and AI standards (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act risk management requirements)
on_scope_evidence: design defect doctrinal tests (consumer expectations test, risk-utility/risk-benefit balancing, Restatement (Second) of Torts §402A and Restatement (Third) formulations)
precedents where absence of a known safety feature was held a design defect (airbags, seatbelts, machine guards, child-resistant packaging)
current technical state of AI supervision: guardrail frameworks, output filters, red-teaming pipelines, runtime anomaly detection, kill-switches and rollback mechanisms
documented AI harm incidents (AI Incident Database entries, biased hiring tools, harmful chatbot outputs, autonomous vehicle crashes)
feasibility and cost data for implementing supervisor functions across AI system classes
standards mapping: NIST AI RMF 'Manage' function, EU AI Act Article 9 risk management system, ISO/IEC 42001 controls
consumer expectation survey data on AI safety features
doctrine on whether software and AI count as a 'product' versus a service for liability purposes
evidence of feasible alternative designs and their cost-benefit profiles
key_tensions: presumption vs. feasibility: whether prima facie treatment is justified when anticipating, detecting, and remediating open-ended AI harms may exceed current technical capability (safetyist burden-shifting vs. accelerationist and skeptic feasibility objections)

design defect doctrine vs. mandated architecture: tort law traditionally avoids compelling a single design, so treating absence of a supervisor function as a defect effectively mandates one (skeptic doctrinal objection vs. safetyist analogy to airbags and crumple zones)
innovation burden vs. safety duty: compliance costs, slowed deployment, and defensive engineering versus the social cost of unremediated harms (accelerationist vs. safetyist)

defining 'AI harms': whether harms must be concrete, foreseeable, and user-specific or can include diffuse societal harms — which determines whether a coherent supervisor-function requirement can exist at all
off_scope_topics: whether AI development should be paused, banned, or accelerated as a general matter
specific model architectures and training methods discussed for their own sake
legislative licensing regimes, international treaties, or new regulatory agencies (policy instruments other than tort liability)
interchangeable liability theories: failure to warn, negligence per se, platform immunity debates
existential or civilizational-scale AI risk scenarios
labor market displacement as a standalone policy issue
military AI and autonomous weapons governed by separate legal regimes
general critiques of capitalism or corporate ethics
drift_signatures: arguing developers are morally or commercially reckless without testing the claim against design-defect elements (feasible alternative design, risk-utility balance, consumer expectations)
proposing licensing regimes, moratoria, or new statutes instead of evaluating the tort-law design defect claim
recounting individual AI harm incidents in detail without linking them to the anticipate/detect/remediate functions at issue
debating AGI timelines, superintelligence, or existential risk rather than litigable product harms
substituting failure-to-warn or negligence analysis as if it were interchangeable with the design defect question
detailing model internals (training data, RLHF, architectures) with no connection to supervisor-function feasibility or cost
scope.example_ceiling: Litigable product-liability scale: documented AI incidents with identifiable harms (discriminatory outputs, injurious chatbot content, physical injury or death from autonomous systems) and design-defect precedents from mature industries; systemic multi-victim failures such as discriminatory deployment at scale remain proportionate, but speculative existential or civilizational scenarios exceed scope
scope.domain: products liability law applied to AI systems; AI safety engineering
scope.product_type: AI systems broadly — the claim spans all AI systems and is not limited to a specific product category
scope.time_horizon: present-day (implied by the present tense 'constitutes' — a claim about current liability doctrine and currently deployable systems)
excluded_scenarios: AI systems that already incorporate a safety supervisor function (definitional boundary of the claim)
